column2: From al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī, the grandson of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his sweet basil (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: I memorised from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: “Leave what makes you doubt for what does not make you doubt.”
Reported by al-Nasāʾī and al-Tirmidhī, who said: good and authentic (ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ).

This hadith was recorded by Imam Aḥmad, al-Tirmidhī, al-Nasāʾī, Ibn Ḥibbān in his Ṣaḥīḥ, and al-Ḥākim, from the hadith of Burayd ibn Abī Maryam, from Abū al-Ḥawrāʾ, from al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī; al-Tirmidhī graded it authentic. As for Abū al-Ḥawrāʾ al-Saʿdī,

most say that his name was Rabīʿah ibn Shaybān, and al-Nasāʾī and Ibn Ḥibbān declared him reliable. Aḥmad hesitated over whether Abū al-Ḥawrāʾ was Rabīʿah ibn Shaybān, and inclined to distinguish the two; and al-Jūzajānī said: Abū al-Ḥawrāʾ is unknown; no one knows him.

This hadith is part of a long hadith that mentions the qunūt of witr. Al-Tirmidhī and others have an addition to it: “For truthfulness is tranquillity, and falsehood is doubt.” Ibn Ḥibbān's wording is: “For good is tranquillity, and evil is doubt.”
Imam Aḥmad recorded it, with a chain containing an unknown narrator, from Anas, that the Prophet ﷺ said:
“Leave what makes you doubt for what does not make you doubt.” He also recorded it by another, better route as mawqūf (the words of Anas himself).
Al-Ṭabarānī recorded it in the narration of Mālik, from Nāfiʿ, from Ibn ʿUmar, as marfūʿ (the Prophet's words). Al-Dāraquṭnī said:
It is narrated only as the words of Ibn ʿUmar, and from ʿUmar, and it is narrated from Mālik as his own words. End of quotation.
It is narrated with a weak chain from ʿUthmān ibn ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī — who is weak — from his father, from al-Ḥasan, from Abū Hurayrah,
that the Prophet ﷺ said to a man: “Leave what makes you doubt for what does not make you doubt.” He said: And how am I to know that?

He said: “When you intend something, put your hand on your chest, for the heart is troubled by the unlawful and at rest with the lawful; and the scrupulous Muslim leaves a small sin for fear of a great one.”
It is also narrated from ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī as a mursal report.
Al-Ṭabarānī recorded something similar, with a weak chain, from Wāthilah ibn al-Asqaʿ, from the Prophet ﷺ, with the addition: He was asked: Then who is the scrupulous one?
He said: “The one who stops at what is doubtful.”

These words have also been narrated as mawqūf sayings of a number of Companions, among them ʿUmar, Ibn ʿUmar and Abū al-Dardāʾ. Ibn Masʿūd said: Why would you want what makes you doubt, when around you are four thousand things that do not make you doubt?
ʿUmar said: Leave usury and what is dubious (rībah) — meaning whatever you have doubts about, even if you are not sure that it is usury.
The meaning of this hadith comes down to stopping at doubtful matters and guarding against them. For the purely lawful produces no unease (rayb) in a believer's heart — rayb

meaning disquiet and agitation; rather, the soul is at rest with it and the heart is tranquil with it. Doubtful things, on the other hand, produce in hearts the disquiet and agitation that give rise to doubt.
Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-ʿUmarī the ascetic said: When a servant is scrupulous, he leaves what makes him doubt for what does not make him doubt.
Al-Fuḍayl said: People claim that scrupulousness is hard; yet whenever two matters have come to me, I have taken the harder of the two. So leave what makes you doubt for what does not make you doubt.
Ḥassān ibn Abī Sinān said: Nothing is easier than scrupulousness: if something makes you doubt, leave it.
But this is easy only for the likes of Ḥassān (may Allah have mercy on him).
Ibn al-Mubārak said: An agent of Ḥassān ibn Abī Sinān wrote to him from al-Ahwāz: The sugar cane has been struck by blight, so buy up sugar where you are. He bought it from a man,
and before long there was a profit of thirty thousand on what he had bought. He went to the owner of the sugar and said: My man had written to me,

and I did not tell you; so cancel the sale I made with you. The other said to him: You have told me now, and I have made it lawful for you. He went back, but his heart could not bear it, so he went to him again and said:
I did not come at this matter in the proper way, and I would like you to take this sale back. He kept at him until the man took it back.

When there was demand for goods and they were selling well, and Yūnus ibn ʿUbayd sent someone to buy them, he would tell the person buying for him: Let the one you buy from know that the goods are in demand.
Hishām ibn Ḥassān said: Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn gave up forty thousand over something in which you today see no harm.

Al-Ḥajjāj ibn Dīnār sent grain to al-Baṣrah with a man and told him to sell it on the day he arrived, at that day's price. Then a letter came from the man: I reached al-Baṣrah and found grain in poor demand, so I held it back. The price of grain then rose,

and I made such-and-such more on it. Al-Ḥajjāj wrote to him: You have betrayed us and acted against what we told you. When my letter reaches you, give the entire price of that grain in charity to the poor of al-Baṣrah — and I only wish I may come out of it safe once you have done so.

Yazīd ibn Zurayʿ kept himself clear of five hundred thousand from his father's inheritance and did not take it, because his father used to hold offices for the rulers. Yazīd used to weave palm leaves and lived on that until he died (may Allah have mercy on him).
Al-Miswar ibn Makhramah had hoarded a great deal of grain. He saw clouds in the autumn and disliked the sight, and said: Do I not see that I have come to dislike what benefits the Muslims?
So he swore that he would make no profit from it at all. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb was told of this, and ʿUmar said to him: May Allah reward you with good.
This shows that a hoarder should keep himself clear of the profit on what he has hoarded in a forbidden way.
Imam Aḥmad (may Allah have mercy on him) stated explicitly that one should keep clear of profit on what has not come under one's liability, since it falls under profit on what one has not guaranteed,
which the Prophet ﷺ forbade. In one reported position, Aḥmad said about someone who leases out at a profit what he has himself leased: He gives the profit in charity.
In another reported position he said about the profit on capital in a muḍārabah partnership when the working partner has gone against its terms: He gives it in charity.

In another he said about someone who buys fruit before it is ripe on condition that it be cut, and then leaves it until it ripens: He gives the increase in charity. A group of scholars of our school took this as recommended,
because giving away doubtful things in charity is recommended.
It is narrated that ʿĀʾishah (may Allah be pleased with her) was asked about someone in iḥrām eating game, and said: They are only a few days, so whatever makes you doubt, leave it — meaning:
whatever you are unsure of, whether it is lawful or unlawful, leave it. For people have differed over whether someone in iḥrām may eat game that he did not hunt himself.
This may be cited as evidence that keeping clear of scholarly disagreement is better,
because it is further from doubt. But the scholars who examine things closely, of our school and others, hold that this is not unrestricted,

for among disputed questions are some in which a concession is established from the Prophet ﷺ with nothing opposing it; following that concession is better than avoiding it, even if it did not reach some scholars,
who refrained from it for that reason. An example is someone who is certain of his purity and doubts whether he has become impure; for it is authentically reported that the Prophet ﷺ said:

“He should not leave until he hears a sound or smells a smell” — especially if his doubt arises during the prayer, for he may not break it off, since the prohibition of that is authentic, even though some scholars make it obligatory.

If the concession has something opposing it, whether another Sunnah or the practice of the Ummah to the contrary, it is better not to act on it. The same holds if a few isolated people acted on it while the contrary practice was widespread in the Ummah, in the lands of the Muslims, from the time of the Companions;

for then adopting what the Muslims practise is the only course, since Allah has protected this Ummah from having the people of falsehood within it prevail over the people of truth. Whatever practice prevailed in the three excellent generations is the truth, and anything else is falsehood.
There is a point here that should be noted: exactitude in holding back from doubtful matters is fitting only for someone whose states are all upright
and whose deeds are of a piece in taqwā and scrupulousness. As for someone who indulges in violating manifest prohibitions and then wants to be scrupulous about some subtle doubtful matter,

that is not to be borne from him; on the contrary, he is to be rebuked for it. As Ibn ʿUmar said of the people of Iraq, when one of them asked him about the blood of mosquitoes: They ask me about the blood of mosquitoes when they have killed al-Ḥusayn! And I heard the Prophet ﷺ say: “They are my two sweet basils from this world.”
A man asked Bishr ibn al-Ḥārith about a man who has a wife and whose mother tells him to divorce her. He said: If he has been dutiful to his mother in everything,
and nothing of his duty to her remains but divorcing his wife, let him do it. But if he is dutiful to her by divorcing his wife and then afterwards goes and beats his mother, he should not do it.

Imam Aḥmad (may Allah have mercy on him) was asked about a man who buys greens and stipulates that the palm-leaf strip be included — meaning the one with which the bunch of greens is tied. Aḥmad said: What sort of questions are these?!
He was told: It is Ibrāhīm ibn Abī Nuʿaym who asks. Aḥmad said: If it is Ibrāhīm ibn Abī Nuʿaym, then yes: this suits a man like him.
He objected to such questions only from someone whose state did not match them; for the people of exacting scrupulousness, this does match their state.
Imam Aḥmad himself practised this scrupulousness. He once told someone to buy him some ghee, and the man brought it on a leaf, so he ordered the leaf to be returned to the seller.

Imam Aḥmad would not dip his pen in his companions' inkwells; he would bring out his own inkwell and dip from that. A man asked his permission to write from his inkwell, and he said to him: Write — this is a dark kind of scrupulousness. Another man asked his permission for the same, and he smiled and said:
Neither my scrupulousness nor yours has reached this. He said this out of humility; in fact he practised this scrupulousness himself,
but he objected to it from someone who had not reached that station but was lax about manifest disliked things and rushed into doubtful matters without hesitation.
His words ﷺ, “For good is tranquillity and evil is doubt,” mean that hearts are tranquil with good, while evil makes them uneasy and they find no tranquillity in it.
This points to referring to one's heart when things are unclear. More will be said on this under the hadith of al-Nawwās ibn Samʿān, if Allah the Exalted wills.
Ibn Jarīr recorded with his chain from Qatādah, from Bushayr ibn Kaʿb, that he recited this verse:

“So walk through its tracts (manākib)” [al-Mulk 67:15]. Then he said to his slave girl: If you know what its manākib are, you are free for the sake of Allah. She said: Its manākib are its mountains. His face fell as if he had been struck, for he wanted to keep his slave girl,

so he asked people about it; some told him to free her and some told him not to. Then he asked Abū al-Dardāʾ, who said: Good is tranquillity and evil is doubt; so leave what makes you doubt for what does not make you doubt.
His words in the other narration, “Truthfulness is tranquillity and falsehood is doubt,” indicate that one should not rely on what just anyone says, as he said in the hadith of Wābiṣah:

“…even if people give you a fatwa, and give you a fatwa.” One should rely only on the words of someone who speaks the truth. The sign of truth is that hearts are tranquil with it, and the sign of falsehood is that it produces doubt, so that hearts do not rest with it but recoil from it.

That is why, in the time of the Prophet ﷺ, intelligent people who heard his words and what he called to knew that he was truthful and had brought the truth; and when they heard the words of Musaylimah they knew that he was lying

and had brought falsehood. It is narrated that ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ, before he became Muslim, heard him claim that this had been revealed to him: “O hyrax, O hyrax, you have two ears and a chest,” and [he added]: “You surely know, ʿAmr.” ʿAmr said: By Allah, I know that you are lying.

One of the early scholars said: Picture in your heart whatever you wish and reflect on it, then set it against its opposite; when you distinguish between the two, you will know truth from falsehood and truthfulness from lying. He said: For instance, you picture Muḥammad ﷺ

and then reflect on the Qurʾān he brought, and recite: “In the creation of the heavens and the earth, the alternation of night and day, and the ships that sail the sea with what benefits people…” [al-Baqarah 2:164];
then you picture the opposite of Muḥammad ﷺ and find it to be Musaylimah, and reflect on what he brought, and recite:
Come, lady of the inner chamber, / the bed has been made ready for you!
These were his words to Sajāḥ when he married her. He said: You find this — meaning the Qurʾān — firm and wondrous, clinging to the heart and beautiful to the ear;
and you find that — meaning Musaylimah's words — cold, insipid and obscene. Then you know that Muḥammad was truly given revelation, and that Musaylimah was a liar who was given falsehood.
